Hi @LuckyTriple7, thanks for the rebase. The conflict is cleared and both HACS and hassfest are green on the current release, so here is the proper pass.

Two notes before the findings. The PR body still links `v0.5.0` and the action runs from back then, while the repository is on `v0.24.0`; please update it. And I reviewed against `v0.24.0`, where the entity accounting is exact: 37 documented in the README table and 37 shipped, no undocumented entity and nothing documented that does not exist.

## Blocker: the declared floor is about twenty-five releases below what the code needs

`hacs.json` declares `"homeassistant": "2024.1.0"`. `__init__.py` line 65 reads `lovelace.resource_mode`.

I counted occurrences of `resource_mode` in core's `homeassistant/components/lovelace/__init__.py`: zero at 2026.1.0, six at 2026.2.0. The field was `mode` before that and only became `resource_mode` in 2026.2.0. The compatibility shims on `LovelaceData` cover subscript and `.get()` access, not attribute access, so on 2026.1.0 this raises `AttributeError` inside the `async_at_started` callback rather than degrading.

There are three more constraints below it, all above your declared floor: `LOVELACE_DATA` in `lovelace/const.py` is absent through 2025.1.0 and first present at 2025.2.0, and the import at line 62 is not guarded, so below that it is a hard `ImportError`; `StaticPathConfig` needs 2024.7.0; and the implicit `OptionsFlow.config_entry` you read at `config_flow.py` lines 207, 242 and 265 needs 2024.12.0.

So the true floor is `2026.2.0`. Everything between the declared 2024.1.0 and 2025.1.x fails at import, and everything from 2025.2.0 to 2026.1.x fails with `AttributeError`.

## Blocker: the integration writes the user's Lovelace resource store and never cleans up

`__init__.py` lines 51 to 85 reach into `hass.data[LOVELACE_DATA]`, force the store to load with `resources.async_get_info()`, iterate `resources.async_items()`, and then call `resources.async_update_item(...)` or `resources.async_create_item(...)`.

That is the shared, user-owned `.storage/lovelace_resources`. A config entry setting itself up should not be editing it.

Your comment at lines 52 to 60 makes a real argument, and I want to acknowledge it: `frontend.add_extra_js_url` does get rendered behind an `isModern` user-agent check, and on a browser that check rejects, the card silently fails to load. That is a genuine problem and you diagnosed it correctly. But the answer is to ship the card as a separate `plugin` submission, where HACS writes the resource as the package manager acting on the user's behalf and the user knows it happened, rather than to have an integration write it behind their back.

There is a second, independent problem with the current approach. The URL carries `?v={CARD_VERSION}`, so lines 79 to 82 rewrite the entry on every version bump, and there is no removal path at all: no `async_remove_entry` anywhere in the tree and no `async_delete_item` call. Uninstalling the integration leaves an orphaned resource pointing at a dead `/beach_weather_static/...` URL, which Lovelace then tries to load on every dashboard render, forever, on an installation that no longer has the integration.

## All 37 entities hardcode their entity ID

`sensor.py` lines 192, 894, 982, 1002 and 1062, `button.py` line 41, `weather.py` line 171.

The comment at `sensor.py` lines 971 and 972 says this is to keep existing picture-elements cards working, so I know it is deliberate. It still takes ownership of something the entity registry is meant to derive, it means a user's own rename does not survive, and it sits oddly next to `_attr_has_entity_name = True` on the same classes, which is the mechanism that would otherwise do the naming.

## Smaller items

- The card editor interpolates registry names into `innerHTML` without escaping: `beach-weather-card.js` lines 703 to 710 for the device name and lines 825 to 833 for the entity friendly name. Both trace back to the user's own ty

payload.body:
Hi @rdgerken, thanks for the quick rebase back on 1 August. Here is the proper pass I owed you.

I reviewed against `v0.4.1`, which is what the PR body links and is the current release. The counting all lines up: two services documented and two shipped and two in `strings.json`, nine config fields against nine strings, ten options against ten, five flow errors against five, two repair issues with matching placeholders. That level of internal consistency is not common in this queue.

## Blocker: the statistics import raises `TypeError` on every version from your declared floor up to 2025.10

`statistics.py` line 217, inside `_metadata()`:

```python
"unit_class": None,  # no unit conversion (required key on newer HA)
```

That dict goes straight into `async_add_external_statistics` at lines 265 and 308. I traced where it lands in core: `async_add_external_statistics` does no key filtering, the recorder task reaches `statistics_meta.py` `_add_metadata`, which calls `StatisticsMeta.from_meta(new_metadata)`, and `from_meta` in `db_schema.py` is literally `return StatisticsMeta(**meta)`. No filtering anywhere on the path.

`unit_class` is not a column on that model until 2025.11.0. I counted occurrences in `db_schema.py` at both tags: zero at 2025.10.0, one at 2025.11.0, where it appears in `_StatisticsMeta` between `unit_of_measurement` and `has_mean`.

So on 2025.4 through 2025.10, SQLAlchemy's declarative constructor gets an unmapped keyword and raises `TypeError`, in the recorder thread, on both the measurement and the counter path. That is the whole "Import (Timebase to HA)" half of the integration, on every version you say you support.

`hacs.json` declares `2025.4.0` and the v0.4.0 notes say "Minimum Home Assistant: 2025.4". The true floor is `2025.11.0`.

The interesting part is that you already have the right pattern one section up: the comment at line 47 says "StatisticMeanType landed in HA 2025.4", and lines 48 to 54 guard that import with a `try`/`except ImportError` shim. `unit_class` was added later with the comment "required key on newer HA" and no equivalent guard. Either bump the floor to 2025.11.0, or set the key conditionally the same way you handle `StatisticMeanType`.

Your test suite never calls `async_add_external_statistics`, only the pure `accumulate_counter`, which is why CI stayed green through this.

## A rotated Pulse secret produces an endless retry loop

`ConfigEntryAuthFailed`, `async_step_reauth` and even the string `reauth` appear nowhere in the tree. A 401 or 403 from the historian becomes a `TimebaseApiError`, which is a `TimebaseError`, and that is converted to `ConfigEntryNotReady` at `__init__.py` lines 120 and 121 during setup, or to `UpdateFailed` at `sensor.py` line 65 during an update.

So when someone rotates or revokes the Pulse client secret, Home Assistant retries forever with no repair notification and no prompt to re-enter it. The config flow has only `async_step_user`, so the only way back is to delete and re-add the entry. Raising `ConfigEntryAuthFailed` on 401 and 403 and adding a reauth step is the fix.

## The buffer drop policy is not the one you documented

`const.py` line 35 says "oldest dropped beyond this", the docstring at `exporter.py` line 242 says "Drop oldest samples", and both `strings.json` and the README tell the user "the oldest samples were dropped". The implementation at lines 244 to 253 is:

```python
while self._buffered_count > MAX_BUFFERED_TVQS:
    for tag, tvqs in self._buffer.items():
        if tvqs:
            tvqs.pop(0)
            ...
            break
```

The inner loop always lands on the first non-empty tag in insertion order and pops that tag's oldest sample, then starts over. Under sustained overflow it drains the earliest-registered tag completely before touching any other, rather than dropping the globally oldest sample across tags. So one entity loses its whole buffered history while later-registered entities lose nothing, which is not what

payload.body:
Hi @fabiomatavelli, this is good work. Merging it. Three small things for a future release, none of them blocking: - `diagnostics.py` line 13 puts `DevSN` in `TO_REDACT` and applies it to `entry_data` and `raw_data`, but `parsed_data` at line 27 goes out unredacted, and `profiles.py` line 154 writes that same serial into it as `serial_number`. So the serial is hidden in two places and printed in the third. Diagnostics files get pasted into public issue threads, so adding `serial_number` to the set and wrapping `parsed_data` is worth doing. - `invert_current_sign` (`config_flow.py` lines 159 to 161) defaults to on and flips the sign of the current and power sensors, and the README never mentions it. It is explained properly in the Configure dialog through `strings.json`, so nobody is left stranded, but a default that changes what the sensors report deserves a line in the docs. - `brand/dark_icon.png` and `brand/dark_icon@2x.png` are byte identical to their light counterparts, same git blob on each pair, so they add about 300 KB to every download without giving a dark theme anything. There is also no `logo.png`. Worth noting too that in-tree `brand/` assets are only read from Home Assistant 2026.3 onward, so users on your declared 2025.1.0 floor will not see them at all; `home-assistant/brands` is the place that works everywhere. One thing I want to call out because it is the single most common defect I see in this queue and you got it right: `coordinator.py` raises `UpdateFailed` cleanly out of a handler that does nothing else, so a failing battery actually goes unavailable instead of quietly serving yesterday's state of charge. Welcome to the default store. ../Frenck

                       

Blogging my personal ramblings at frenck.dev

Hi @tieskuh, thanks for the rebase; the conflict is cleared and it merges clean now. Here is the proper pass.

I reviewed against `v0.3.2`. Seven entities documented in the README table and seven shipped, with the enabled-by-default column matching exactly. Release notes all check out against code. The `hacs.json` floor of `2024.8.0` is correct and slightly conservative, since `entry.runtime_data` puts the real floor at 2024.6.0. The `proto/` directory documenting how you derived the protocol is a genuinely nice thing to ship. Nothing in the security sweep came back positive.

Two things, and both come down to the same shape: a bike that is failing looks like a bike that is asleep.

## A persistently failing bike is indistinguishable from a healthy one

`coordinator.py` lines 132 to 156. The poll body catches `ComoduleAuthError` at line 146 and logs a warning, catches `BleakError` at line 149 and logs at debug, and then line 156 is `return self.data` on every path including both failure paths. Nothing propagates.

Core's `ActiveBluetoothDataUpdateCoordinator` sets `last_poll_successful = False` and logs the failure only when the poll method raises, so with nothing raised that flag stays `True` forever and the built in failure and recovery reporting never fires.

That would be survivable on its own, except for what sits on top of it. `entity.py` lines 47 and 48 short-circuit `available` to `True` for anything carrying `always_available`, which is battery, last seen and connectivity. And `binary_sensor.py` line 47 computes Connectivity as `coordinator.available or coordinator.streaming`, where `coordinator.available` is core's passive coordinator property meaning only "an advertisement was seen recently".

So a bike whose auth handshake is rejected every time still advertises, so Connectivity reads on, and battery keeps showing whatever it read before, and neither ever goes unavailable. The README at lines 36 and 37 sells Connectivity as the entity that "tells you whether the reading is live or the last-known one", and in this case it says live while the reading is not.

Credit where it is due: `coordinator.py` lines 163 and 164 only advance `last_successful_poll` when a register actually answered, so Last seen does correctly stop moving. That is the one honest signal, and it is why I rate this worth fixing rather than serious. Letting `ComoduleAuthError` propagate would be enough on its own, since that is the failure mode a user cannot recover from without knowing about it.

## The README promises debug output that no code produces

README lines 178 and 179: "The debug log includes the raw register packets, which is exactly what's needed to map a new model", with the logger YAML at lines 171 to 176.

There are eight `_LOGGER` calls in the component, at `comodule.py` line 199 and `coordinator.py` lines 139, 147, 149, 155, 208 and 222, and every one logs an exception string. None logs a packet. The packets do exist, at `comodule.py` line 124 where `data.raw[key] = packet.hex(" ")`, but that field is never logged, never exposed as an attribute, and there is no diagnostics platform to surface it.

This matters more than a typical doc slip because it is also the documented route for anyone wanting to add a new bike model, and following it produces nothing useful. Either log `data.raw` at debug or add a `diagnostics.py` that returns it.

## Smaller items

- `proto/probe.py` lines 17 to 19 look like real BLE MAC addresses in the usage examples, most likely your own bike. That directory never reaches a user, since `content_in_root: false` means HACS installs only the component, so this is privacy housekeeping rather than a defect. I mention it because `.gitignore` lines 7 and 8 show you were already thinking about not publishing them.
- README line 4 still lists "charging" among the readings, while lines 80 to 84 explain plainly that there is no charging sensor and why. Stale copy in the opening sentence.

payload.body:
Hi @AboveColin, thanks for the rebase. All twelve checks are green on the head, so here is the proper pass.

I reviewed against `v1.0.1`, which is what the PR body links and is the current release. Sixteen entities documented in the release notes, sixteen shipped, sixteen translation keys, one to one with no orphans in either direction. The backing library is properly published to PyPI and exactly pinned, diagnostics has a real `TO_REDACT`, there is a working reauth flow, and the whole security sweep came back clean.

Four things.

## `hacs.json` declares no version floor

The whole file is:

```json
{
  "name": "Basic-Fit",
  "content_in_root": false
}
```

`config_flow.py` line 134 calls `self.async_update_reload_and_abort(...)`. That method is absent from core at 2023.12.0 and 2024.1.0 and first appears in 2024.2.0; I checked the tags directly. `sensor.py` lines 50 and 51 subclass `SensorEntityDescription` with `@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)`, which needs 2024.1.0. So `"homeassistant": "2024.2.0"` is the accurate floor. Without it, HACS offers this to every version and a user below that gets an `AttributeError` on the reauth path instead of a clean "needs a newer Home Assistant".

## A failure on the badges endpoint writes a real zero into long-term statistics

`__init__.py` lines 75 to 89 wrap three optional calls in their own handlers:

```python
try:
    badges = await self.client.get_badges()
except BasicFitError as err:
    _LOGGER.debug("Badges unavailable: %s", err)
    badges = []
```

`sensor.py` lines 213 to 220 then does `value_fn=lambda d: len(d.get("badges") or [])` with `state_class=SensorStateClass.TOTAL`. So any transient failure on that one endpoint, a timeout included, records a hard `0` badges into the statistics table rather than leaving the sensor unknown. The four measurement sensors degrade to `None` and are fine; it is only the count that turns an error into a plausible-looking number. Returning `None` when badges could not be fetched fixes it.

There is a narrower second edge in the same block. I pulled the `basicfit` wheel to check the hierarchy, and `exceptions.py` has `class BasicFitAuthError(BasicFitError)`, so those three inner handlers catch auth errors too and they never reach the `except BasicFitAuthError` at line 90 that raises `ConfigEntryAuthFailed`. A fully dead token still triggers reauth correctly, because `get_member` runs outside the inner blocks and fails first. But an endpoint-scoped 401, say a revoked scope on measurements, is invisible forever. Your own package docstring says the hierarchy exists "so callers (including the Home Assistant integration) can tell authentication problems apart", so re-raising `BasicFitAuthError` ahead of the inner catches is what it was built for.

## The config entry is keyed on the member's display name

`config_flow.py` line 97:

```python
await self.async_set_unique_id(str(data.get(CONF_MEMBER_NAME) or title))
```

Two people with the same name cannot both be added, and a real person's name ends up as the entry's unique id in the registry. A membership or account id would be a better key.

Related, line 126 onwards: the reauth step does not check that the re-authenticated account is the same one. Without `_abort_if_unique_id_mismatch`, someone who reauths with a different Basic-Fit login silently rebinds the entry, and the previous member's visit history carries on under the new account's entities.

## The brand folder does not do what the release notes say

The `v1.0.1` notes say the bundled assets were added "so HACS brand validation passes for default-store inclusion". `home-assistant/brands` has no `basic_fit` entry under either `core_integrations/` or `custom_integrations/`, both 404, and nothing in the repository references the `brand/` directory. Home Assistant and HACS resolve brand imagery from that repository, never from a folder inside the component.

So the four PNGs under `custom_components/basic_fit/brand/` are 603,734 bytes

Hi @mrtian2016, thanks for pushing again; the conflict is resolved and the entry merges cleanly at the right sort position. Here is the proper pass.

I reviewed against `v0.6.0`. The PR body still links `v0.3.0` and the action run from that era, three releases back, so please refresh both.

This is one of the tighter submissions I have looked at in a while. Every entity translation key has a shipped entity behind it and vice versa, 56 for 56 with no orphans in either direction; `services.yaml` matches `services.py` field for field; `ConfigEntryAuthFailed` is raised where it should be and there is a real reauth flow behind it; `available` consults `last_update_success` everywhere; diagnostics has a proper `TO_REDACT` with a suffix safety net; all three views are `requires_auth = True`; unique IDs are entry scoped throughout; and there are no runtime dependencies at all. The commit messages naming the exact Home Assistant versions each change was verified against are genuinely useful.

Two things.

## The declared floor is one release too low, and it breaks the options flow on the version you advertise

`hacs.json` declares `"homeassistant": "2024.11.0"`, README line 63 says 2024.11 or newer, and `requirements-test.txt` agrees.

`config_flow.py` line 63 returns `YunkanOptionsFlow()` with no arguments, and line 187 reads `self.config_entry.options`.

The base `OptionsFlow` did not have a `config_entry` attribute at 2024.11.0. I dumped the class body at that tag to be certain: it contains a `handler: str` annotation and `_async_abort_entries_match`, nothing else, and `ConfigEntryBaseFlow` adds only `_flow_result`. `data_entry_flow.py` at 2024.11.0 has no `config_entry` anywhere either. The only `config_entry` property at that tag lives on `OptionsFlowWithConfigEntry`, which requires the entry to be passed in. It moves onto the base class in 2024.12.0.

So on exactly the version this project advertises as its minimum, pressing Configure raises `AttributeError` at `config_flow.py` line 187.

Everything else genuinely does land on 2024.11.0, which is presumably how this slipped past: the `config_entry=` kwarg on `DataUpdateCoordinator`, `_get_reauth_entry`, and the native WebRTC provider API (`camera/webrtc.py` is a 404 at 2024.10.0 and present at 2024.11.0) all arrived there. The options flow is the one thing that needs one more release. `"homeassistant": "2024.12.0"` in `hacs.json`, plus README line 63 and `requirements-test.txt`.

To be clear about the other half of this: constructing the options flow with no arguments and never assigning `self.config_entry` is exactly right, and is what keeps you working on 2025.12 and later where the setter was removed. The fix is only the declared minimum.

## The event snapshot view is missing the camera scoping its two siblings have

`views.py` lines 88 to 122, `YunkanEventSnapshotView`. It validates that `path` is truthy, starts with `events/` and has no `..`, then proxies it upstream with the integration's backend token. It never checks that the event belongs to a camera this integration exposes.

Both siblings do check, and your own comments say why. Line 79 to 83 on the camera snapshot view: "Without this, any authenticated HA user could borrow the integration's backend token to snapshot a hidden camera by id", enforced at line 82. Line 148 to 153 on the recording view: "a recording belonging to a hidden camera must not be reachable by guessing its (sequential) id", enforced at line 152.

The v0.3.0 commit message claims "snapshot/recording proxies scoped to exposed cameras (anti-IDOR)". The event snapshot proxy is the hole in that claim. `media_source.py` lines 69 to 85 resolve `img/<event_id>` through `async_get_event` and sign a URL with the same absence of an ownership check.
